title: Live w/ Colette Molteni and Giulia Scalaberni - Why some leaders treat Psychological Safety as Soft
author: Colette Molteni and Giulia Scalaberni
summary: Colette Molteni's write-up of her live conversation with Giulia Scalaberni, who leads a distributed team across Europe and India, argues that psychological safety is load-bearing rather than soft because it determines whether leaders hear about problems while they can still be fixed. The piece distills five lessons. Trust runs on different protocols in different cultures, delivery-first in many European teams and relationship-first in India, so Scalaberni paused a tight timeline for a session of introductions. Bad news should be deliverable as if over coffee rather than while fleeing a fire, with the leader acting as a filter for pressure. Teams mixing cultures must write down what normal means, as her team did in a ten-point manifesto that made reporting a broken platform an act of contribution. Silence should be read as data rather than agreement, given pauses that range from three to nine seconds across cultures. And the leader, like a DJ, owns noticing disengagement. The closing claim is that what goes unsaid in the room still sends a bill later, with interest.
points: Scalaberni found European delivery-first trust stalled with her Indian colleagues, for whom relationship came before the work.
Her team's co-written ten-point manifesto reframed reporting a broken platform as contribution rather than accusation.
Differences in conversational pause length across cultures mean silence after a question should prompt another channel, not be taken as assent.
The DJ metaphor places responsibility for spotting masked disengagement squarely on the leader, as feedback on their own leadership.
quotes: What most people miss is that psychological safety decides whether you hear about a problem while you can still fix it, or after it has already cost you.
Trust there was relationship-first: who you are, your family, what you do on the weekend. Only then does the work start.
Giulia’s metaphor: people should be able to bring you bad news the way they would over coffee, not while running from a burning building.
With cultures mixed on one team, directness can read as rudeness and silence can read as agreement.
When you can’t assume shared norms, you have to declare them.
Whose job is it to notice when someone starts wearing a mask? Giulia was clear: the leader’s. If the room stops dancing, you change the track.
And one line I keep coming back to: if something doesn’t get said in the room, the bill still arrives. It just arrives later, with interest.
